opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's hard to say. I'd break it into a few layers.

At the top level, the question is whether there's a good formal notion of heuristic argument at all: something that captures the way mathematicians and physicists reason when they say "these two things look unrelated, so I'll assume they're independent unless I see a reason they aren't." We have a lot of intuitions about how that should behave. It should be defeasible, you should be able to add considerations that change your estimate, and it shouldn't be trivially exploitable. But writing down a definition that has all those properties at once has turned out to be surprisingly subtle. Every time we propose something, we find a counterexample where it gives absurd answers or where an adversary can push the estimate wherever they want.

So how hard is it? I'd put it in the category of problems where I don't think we're missing some deep new mathematics, but where the search space is large and it's easy to spend a long time going in circles. If you'd asked me a few years ago, I'd probably have said there was a decent chance we'd have a satisfying formalization within a few years. That was optimistic. Things have taken longer than I hoped. Some of the obstacles we ran into felt like they might be fundamental, and then on closer inspection they turned out to be about how we'd set up the problem. That's encouraging in one sense, but it also means it's hard to tell how close you are.

Then there's a second layer: even if you have a good definition, can you actually find these heuristic arguments for the systems we care about, like neural networks, efficiently enough to be useful? That's a separate and maybe harder question. The hope is that the arguments are roughly as cheap to find as the models are to train, that you can learn the explanation alongside the model. I think that's plausible, but it's really a conjecture at this point.

If I had to put rough numbers on it, I'd say maybe something like a 20-30% chance this whole program works out in a way that really matters for alignment. That might sound low, but I think it's a pretty good bet compared to the alternatives. The payoff if it works is large: you'd have a principled way of saying "this model is behaving well for the reason we think, not because of some weird coincidence or a treacherous plan." Most of the difficulty is that we're trying to do theory in an area where nobody has really worked out the foundations, so you're kind of inventing the questions as you go.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the work taking longer than expected and obstacles being reframed, but does not state that three person-years of work could be followed by a fresh approach solving an open problem in three to six months.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating a few different things that could be hard about it, because they're hard in pretty different ways.

The basic idea in that paper is that mathematicians and physicists constantly reason in this way where you say, look, I don't see any reason these two things should be correlated, so I'm going to treat them as independent until someone shows me a reason. And that heuristic is doing an enormous amount of work in practice. It's how you get the prime number theorem heuristically before you can prove it, it's how you get the twin prime conjecture, it's how you argue that a random SAT instance is probably unsatisfiable above some threshold. What we wanted was a formal version of that: a set of rules where you start with a default of "no structure," and then there's a well-defined notion of what it means for someone to point out structure, and your estimates update in a principled way when they do.

The thing that makes the open problems feel hard is that we're asking for a bunch of properties simultaneously that are individually easy and jointly very constraining. You want the estimator to be consistent with the actual truth whenever there's a proof, so it can't contradict things you can prove. You want it to be exploitable in the sense that if someone presents an argument that your estimate is wrong, you have to move; you can't just stubbornly ignore evidence. And you want it to be efficiently computable, roughly as cheap as checking the argument that was presented. Any two of those feel fine. Getting all three at once, in a way that handles arbitrary structure rather than the particular examples we understand, is where it gets stuck.

My honest assessment is that I don't know if the core problem is hard in the "this is a deep mathematical obstruction" sense or hard in the "nobody serious has spent two years on it" sense. There's a real chance it's the second. The paper was more of an invitation than a result. We had a bunch of candidate definitions, and for each one we could find a case where it either became degenerate or stopped being tractable, and we couldn't tell whether that was because the definitions were wrong or because the thing we wanted doesn't exist. That's an uncomfortable epistemic state, but it's also where a lot of good problems start.

The reason I care about it, to be clear, is not mostly as a math project. It's that if you want to explain what a neural network is doing, you can't do it by proof. The behaviors are statistical, the networks are enormous, and "prove this model never does X" is going to be false or unprovable for basically any interesting X. So you need some weaker notion of explanation, something like "here is an argument for why the model behaves this way, and the argument accounts for all the structure that matters." And that requires exactly this kind of formalism: a way to say what counts as an explanation, and a way to notice when an explanation is incomplete because the model is relying on a correlation the explanation didn't mention. So the difficulty of the formal problem translates fairly directly into the difficulty of the thing I'd actually like to do with it.

If I had to put rough odds on it, I'd say maybe a third chance that there's a clean, satisfying definition that someone finds in the next several years, a third chance that we end up with a messy patchwork of partial results that's still useful in practice, and a third chance it turns out the right question was slightly different and we were chasing the wrong formalization. I'd be pretty happy with either of the first two outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that three person-years of work could be followed by a fresh approach solving an open problem in three to six months. It instead speculates that the difficulty may reflect limited effort and gives broad odds over the next several years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite hard to assess. With this kind of theoretical work, you can have a fairly clear picture of what you want, and still not know whether you’re missing one good idea or whether the whole approach needs to change.

The basic aspiration is to say when you should treat two things as independent in the absence of an argument that they’re correlated. But the absence of an argument depends on what reasoning you’re able to do. Two quantities could be related in a way that’s obvious to a more powerful reasoner and completely opaque to you. So you want a notion that respects those computational limitations, while still giving sensible answers as you discover more structure.

My uncertainty is less about whether we can write down some formal rule and more about whether we can find one that captures what we actually want. You can propose something, see that it works on a few examples, and then find another example where it behaves badly. The question is whether that process converges on a clean principle.

So I’m hopeful, but I wouldn’t give a confident timeline. I think even a relatively simple formulation that survived serious attempts to break it would be substantial progress.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about whether the approach will converge and declines to give a confident timeline. It does not state that three person-years of prior work could be followed by a fresh approach solving an open problem in three to six months.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different levels of difficulty. At one level, you can write down a principle that captures the intuition in some simple cases: if you don’t have a reason to think two things are correlated, you should treat them as independent. The hard part is saying what counts as a reason, especially when the things you’re reasoning about are mathematical facts and the correlations can follow from computations you haven’t done yet.

For example, you don’t want to assume two quantities are independent if there’s a short argument that they’re equal. But you also can’t require your reasoner to discover every mathematical relationship before it makes any estimates. So you need some account of which relationships it should recognize, and how its estimates should change as it does more reasoning.

My guess is that making progress on concrete versions of that problem is quite tractable. I’m much less confident about getting a single clean formalism that does everything we want. Part of the uncertainty is that we don’t yet know whether we’re missing one conceptual idea or whether there’s a long sequence of complications we’ll have to work through. I’m optimistic that there’s something principled there, but I wouldn’t claim we have a reliable estimate of how far away it is.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses tractable progress and uncertainty about a complete formalism, but does not state that three person-years of work could be compatible with a fresh approach solving an open problem in three to six months.
